text:
BERT4Rec explicitly identifies shifted next-item supervision under bidirectional attention as leakage: the target can remain visible at a later input position. Legitimate Cloze training predicts selected original items at their corresponding corrupted positions using surrounding historical context. Inference appends a reserved [MASK] and reads its hidden state; terminal-mask training reduces this mismatch. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690). The authors’ generator defaults to mask_prob=1.0, replacing every selected target with [MASK]; configurable alternatives retain or randomly replace selected items, so audit the effective corruption policy rather than assuming BERT’s 80/10/10 rule. [Generator](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/gen_data_fin.py).

Proposed independent audit, inferred from these mechanisms: preserve user/source-event indices through cropping, padding and corruption; trace each supervised output position to its original event and label. Verify that shifted labels cannot expose their target event elsewhere in bidirectional input. Distinguish repeated item IDs at different historical events from exposure of the target event itself. For terminal examples, exclude later events; with left padding, read the actual final nonpadding mask position, never count−1. Trace supervision through the actual loss: the reference implementation gathers selected hidden states, computes cross-entropy against aligned labels, applies prediction weights, and passes that loss to the optimizer. Independently recompute loss and verify ignored positions contribute zero direct loss. [Loss implementation](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/run.py).

Reproducibility also depends on convergence: Petrov and Macdonald needed up to 30× longer training with the original implementation. This supports reporting optimization effort separately from leakage correctness; validation performance alone cannot establish supervision integrity. [Replicability study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07483).
